newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Prosecutor demands life for Serb war criminal.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutor demands life for Serb war criminal.

text.p: Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Dusan Tadic should be sentenced to life imprisonment for his actions, prosecutors told the U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Hague on Wednesday.

Tadic, 41, was found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity by the tribunal on May 7 for his part in a Serb "ethnic cleansing" campaign against Bosnian Moslems in 1992. The court is holding hearings ahead of sentencing on July 14.

"We need to ensure that those responsible for these heinous crimes are brought to justice," said prosecutor Grant Niemann. "The most effective way this can be assured with regard to Tadic is to impose upon him a life sentence."
The former bar owner and father of two girls was convicted on 11 counts of persecuting and beating Bosnian Moslems, some of whom he had known for years.

The court cleared him on nine counts of murder -- encompassing 13 deaths -- but found him guilty of two other cold-blooded killings which were not charged individually but included under an umbrella persecution charge.
Niemann said there were no mitigating factors to excuse Tadic's misdeeds.

"It is our submission this was a particularly serious crime, it was an evil crime," he told the court. "Tadic had no reason to do what he did -- he did it out of greed, hatred, jealousy and intolerance."
During his trial, prosecutors portrayed Tadic as fervent Serb nationalist who had rounded up his Moslem neighbours and helped torture, rape and kill them at Serb-run prison camps.
"Tadic was two-faced," Niemann said. "He portrayed himself as friend of the Moslems whilst obviously harbouring a deep hatred for these people, who had extended to him the hand of friendship."

Arrested in Germany in February 1994 while visiting relatives, Tadic has already spent more than three years in custody. He has always denied all charges and his lawyers have already appealed, claiming that he was denied a fair trial.
But Niemann said Tadic had shown no remorse at any stage in the trial and the court should send a message by making sure he got his "just deserts".

"One of the primary functions of the tribunal is to contribute to the restoration of peace in the former Yugoslavia," he said. "This will not be achieved if the tribunal preoccupies itself with rehabilitating individual perpetrators."

The International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia has, in total, indicted 75 war crimes suspects -- 54 Serbs (one of whom has since died), 18 Croats and three Moslems -- but has only nine in its custody.
The judgement in the Tadic case was the first in a full-length trial since the tribunal was set up by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993.
